title: The Goddess in all beings
hookLine: a refrain that never changes, and a list that slips in hunger, sleep and error beside peace and compassion
carry: the goddess dwells in all beings, even hunger

lines: THE ROOM TURNS TO THE GODDESS.
cards: Halfway through the evening, the music changes key and the room turns toward the Goddess. The leader begins a verse with the same ending every time, a run of bows the whole room picks up almost at once.
Only one word in the middle changes. Peace. Faith.
Compassion. Mother. Words that sound right for a hymn to a goddess.
But stay for the whole list, and other words come round too, words nobody would put on a greeting card. Hunger. Sleep.

teach.b: The song comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, set inside the Markandeya Purana.
In its fifth chapter, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken over heaven. The gods, thrown out, go to the Himalaya and praise the Goddess.
Their verse goes like this in Sanskrit: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, then a quality, rupena samsthita, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah.
In paraphrase: to the Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of this, bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, bow, bow. Then they fill in the blank. Consciousness.
Compassion. Mother. And error, bhranti, mistaking one thing for another.
While they sing, Parvati comes to bathe in the river and asks whom they're praising, and from her own body a goddess steps out and answers: this hymn is for me. Then she goes to face the demons.

This is the heart of Shakta teaching, from the Hindus who honor the Goddess as the highest, and many other Hindus share it: Shakti, her power, moves through everything, the bright and the plain alike.
She's in the tired body asking for sleep, the stomach asking for food, even the mind that gets it wrong.
It's why these verses are chanted at Navaratri, the nine nights of the Goddess. Sung as kirtan, the bow at the end never changes, so even someone with no Sanskrit can join from the second verse.
Whatever word comes up, the room bows.

how: The ya devi sarva-bhuteshu verses are recited and sung in Goddess worship, especially during Navaratri, and at kirtans the room often joins the unchanging bow while a leader sings the changing word.

games.q: the Goddess in all beings — tap the pairs.
p: error, mistaking one thing for another

s: the hymn finds the Goddess only in good qualities like peace and faith
it also names sleep, hunger, thirst, shadow and even error.
in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods sing this hymn after being driven from heaven
in its fifth chapter they go to the Himalaya and praise her.
these verses are chanted at Navaratri
the Devi Mahatmya is recited during the nine nights of the Goddess.

games.q: you're one of the gods praising the Goddess in all beings. you've named peace, faith and compassion. does 'error' go on the list?
o: yes. she dwells in error too.
only if it's someone else's error.
games.why: the Devi Mahatmya names bhranti, error, among the forms in which she dwells in all beings, alongside hunger, sleep and thirst.

practice: Check in with the body from the stomach up and name what's here, plainly, one word at a time: hunger, tiredness, thirst, restlessness.
Then name something brighter that's also here, a little patience, a memory, some contentment, without ranking them, letting each word come and go like the changing word in the hymn.
If you pray, follow each word with the hymn's refrain, said silently; if not, notice that both kinds of word belong to the same life.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, to the Goddess in all beings, found in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: namas tasyai, bow to her. The unchanging bow that ends each verse.

carryVoice: Your line: the goddess dwells in all beings, even hunger. Day nine hundred ninety-one, and the Goddess's song is done.
